From Mary Walton's book on W. Edwards Deming (I couldn't quite locate if this is from the 1988 book or the 1990 one):


“In a meeting of two hundred factory workers, a man said to me, ‘It is a matter of communication.’ I hear that word a dozen times a day — communication. I said, ‘Tell me about it.’ His machine had gone out of order and would make only defective items. He had reported it, but the maintenance men could not come for a long time. Meanwhile he was trying to repair it himself. The foreman came along and said to run it. ‘In other words, he told me to make defective items.’

“‘Where is my pride of workmanship?’ he asked me. ‘If the foreman would give me as much respect as he does the machine, I’d be better off.’

comments.author: epidemian
comments.text:
I can only guess the reason people are flagging this. But i would absolutely bet on that guess.

The main issue is not the unkind manner of your post though. It's that you're not addressing the main point of the article. The main point is not that the author is not a software engineer (surprise!). They have probably been employed as a "software engineer" for a long time. The point of the article (IMO, of course) is that their self-exclusion from that title is a reaction to what this industry has become.

In a way, it's saying "this is not engineering; it's nonsense! If this is what being a software engineer has become, then i'm not one".

And personally, i can relate to that feeling. Many many times i've felt that calling what we do as software developers "engineering" is an insult to other engineering disciplines. Mostly for the fact that we call it that, and we still don't give a fuck about what we do. A civil engineer totally gives a fuck about their bridge collapsing; and when a  big collapses happens, the whole industry gives a fuck and reacts and learns how to avoid that from happening in the future. A so-call software "engineer" however, can have production crash time and time again for reasons that are completely preventable, and count it as a success story on their CV.

And you can probably guess what i think about the current trend of software engineering being not giving a fuck about the actual code that we ship, because we delegated the writing of that code to another "intelligence".

I understand why this happens, and i don't want to suggest that i have all the answers about how things should be done. But let's not pretend that this is serious. That this is "engineering".

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
The main point is not that the author is not a software engineer (surprise!). They have probably been employed as a "software engineer" for a long time.


Whether the person is a software engineer or not depends on their location -- in some locations (e.g. Canada ex Alberta) the title of "engineer" is protected, and they (and I) would not be considered software engineers. In other locations a software engineer is anyone who is employed as a programmer, in which case both they and I would be considered software engineers.

The author's problem stems from them trying to derive the qualifications of the term "software engineer" from the opinions of their coworkers, which are irrelevant.


The point of the article (IMO, of course) is that their self-exclusion from that title is a reaction to what this industry has become.


The tech industry is the same as it always has been.

Some people are paid to write programs for which failure would be catastrophic (avionics, automotive firmware, medical devices) and they use rigorous engineering methodologies to mitigate the risk of programming error.

Some people are paid to write programs that can fail with no particular consequence -- video games, social media, most websites --  and their development methodologies encourage shipping code that works "good enough".

The author wants to work at a company that values rigorous engineering and correctness, but they find themselves working at a company that (inferring from the article) values pumping out low-quality LLM-generated code to meet unreasonably short deadlines.

I get that it's frustrating to work somewhere that has a different culture than the place you want to work, but that isn't a problem with "the industry", it's a problem with working at Cat Videos Website Inc. The tech industry is huge!


Many many times i've felt that calling what we do as software developers "engineering" is an insult to other engineering disciplines. Mostly for the fact that we call it that, and we still don't give a fuck about what we do. A civil engineer totally gives a fuck about their bridge collapsing; and when a big collapses happens, the whole industry gives a fuck and reacts and learns how to avoid that from happening in the future. A so-call software "engineer" however, can have production crash time and time again for reasons that are completely preventable, and count it as a success story on their CV.


Going back to the location-specific definition of "software engineer", it sounds like you'd prefer if the world used the Canadian definition, where someone can't call themselves an "engineer" for slapping together a bug-filled Android app any more than they can call themselves a "lawyer" after watching SovCit videos on YouTube.

That's a reasonable thing to want! If you're the kind of software engineer who values the craft and wants to be rewarded for carefully solving a problem (rather than just LLM-ing it until the tests pass) then it makes sense to want to live and work somewhere that you can call yourself "software engineer" and have that term convey your abilities and outlook.

But ... again, it's location specific. Maybe you work somewhere that "software engineer" means 10+ kLoC a day and people who care about the quality of the code they're signing their names to are considered weird aesthetes. You're not going to be happy there. There is no world in which someone who (1) cares about code quality and (2) wants the people around them to care about code quality can be happy working in a feature factory.


And you can probably guess what i think about the current trend of software engineering being not giving a fuck about the actual code that we ship, because we delegated the writing of that code to another "intelligence".


The thing is, I'm not convinced this is a "current trend". The debate about whether (picking a specific geography here) Silicon Valley programmers should be allowed to call themselves "engineers" dates back to at least the '90s. The introduction of LLMs adds a new wrinkle in that the companies who didn't care about quality now really really don't care about quality, but it's not like anyone switched sides. The pro-slop side just became able to produce more slop with fewer people.


But let's not pretend that this is serious. That this is "engineering".


If you want to advocate for professional licensure of software engineers in Silicon Valley then you'd have my vote, but it'll be an uphill battle considering the guy working at the deli next door has a business card identifying them as a "sandwich engineer".
